_meta.note: Editorial data for generated X-vs-Y pages (render_vs_page in build.py). NEUTRAL / fair-comparison framing (2026-06-16): no winner/value-pick language, no savings hooks, symmetric strengths, objective + verifiable. Pricing numbers ALWAYS come from tools.json via the engine — never write prices here (point to the price table instead). EU 2006/114/EC + Czech §2976+/§2984 + US Lanham: objective, verifiable, representative, non-denigrating.

conventions.pair order: slug 'a' = more searched tool (zapier > make > n8n > pipedream > activepieces > automatisch > node-red); page slug = '<a>-vs-<b>.html'; array order = production priority (cross-links pick nearest published pairs from the top)
conventions.winner: slug of the lower-cost tool at the tracked volumes (objective fact from the engine) — used only to phrase the 'When is <other> the better fit?' FAQ. NOT rendered as a badge/recommendation.
conventions.verdict: neutral objective summary for the hero box — state the factual price position + the other tool's genuine strength + the real trade-off; NO 'winner/value pick', NO 'X× cheaper'/savings hooks; point to the price table for figures. May contain plain HTML.
conventions.whyLoser: answer to 'When is <the other tool> the better fit?' — that tool's genuine strengths, symmetric and non-denigrating.
conventions.faq: optional full FAQ override [{q, a-html}]; when absent the generator builds neutral FAQs from data + whyLoser

zapier.opDef: In Zapier, one task = one action step — a 3-step Zap triggered 100 times consumes 300 tasks.
zapier.ctaBlurb: 100 free tasks a month on 2-step Zaps — fine for checking whether your apps are supported.

make.opDef: In Make, one operation = one module execution, counted per module across the scenario.
make.ctaBlurb: 1,000 free ops a month (2 active scenarios) — enough to run a real pilot before paying anything.

n8n.opDef: n8n Cloud counts workflow executions — one run is one execution regardless of step count; self-hosted n8n has no metering at all.
n8n.ctaBlurb: Community Edition is free forever self-hosted; Cloud has a free trial — test a real workflow either way.

pipedream.opDef: In Pipedream, one credit ≈ 30 seconds of compute time (at 256 MB) — billed on execution time, not step count, so a typical run is about one credit.
pipedream.ctaBlurb: Free tier gives 100 credits a month on 3 workflows — enough to validate an integration.

activepieces.opDef: Activepieces doesn't meter runs at all — pricing is per active flow, with unlimited executions.
activepieces.ctaBlurb: 10 active flows free with unlimited runs — a real pilot costs nothing.

automatisch.opDef: Automatisch doesn't meter operations — one flat cloud price, or self-host for free.
automatisch.ctaBlurb: Open source — self-host for free, or take the flat-price cloud plan.

node-red.opDef: Node-RED has no metering — it's open-source software you run on your own hardware.
node-red.ctaBlurb: Free and open source — install and run in minutes on a Pi or VPS.

pairs.verdict: Across the volumes we track, Make is the lower-cost option, while Zapier carries the larger app catalog (9,725 app connectors vs 2,594) and a simpler point-and-click editor. Make trades a steeper learning curve for more visual, field-level control. See the price table below for exact figures — which one fits comes down to whether you need a Zapier-only integration or prefer Make's lower cost and flexibility.
pairs.whyLoser: When breadth or simplicity matters most. With 9,725 app connectors versus Make's 2,594, Zapier is often the only tool that connects a niche CRM or legacy system, and its point-and-click editor plus large template library get non-technical users running fastest.

faq.q: How do Make and Zapier compare on price?
faq.a: Across the volumes we track, Make is the lower-cost option — see the price table above for the exact figures at each level. Zapier bills per task and Make per operation, so both scale with workflow complexity; the per-unit difference is what drives the gap. Prices are taken from each vendor's public pricing page (June 2026).

faq.q: What counts as an operation on each?
faq.a: In Zapier, one task = one action step — a 3-step Zap triggered 100 times consumes 300 tasks. In Make, one operation = one module execution, counted similarly per module. Both count multi-step workflows multiplicatively, so the per-unit price difference is what matters.

faq.q: Can I self-host either of them?
faq.a: No — both are cloud-only. If self-hosting matters to you (cost control, GDPR, data residency), look at n8n or Activepieces instead — see the compare tool.

faq.q: When is Zapier the better fit?
faq.a: When breadth or simplicity matters most: 9,725 app connectors (often the only tool that connects a niche CRM or legacy system), a point-and-click editor, and the largest template library get non-technical users running fastest.
Taken from official pricing pages and verified June 2026. Values marked ~ are estimates for custom enterprise tiers. Every change we record lands in the price changelog.

pairs.verdict: n8n self-hosted is the lower-cost option across these volumes — but only if you run the server yourself: n8n's Community Edition software is free and you pay for hosting (~$8/mo on a small VPS up to ~$66/mo at high volume — infrastructure, not a tool fee). Zapier is the fully-managed, no-code path with the larger catalog (9,725 app connectors) and nothing to host. If nobody on the team wants to run a server, n8n Cloud is the managed comparison. See the table for figures — the real choice is self-host vs managed.
pairs.whyLoser: When you'd rather not run infrastructure. Zapier is fully managed with a no-code editor and 9,725 app connectors, so a non-technical person can build and own automations without engineering — that convenience is what the price covers.

pairs.verdict: Price barely separates these two — n8n self-hosted (from ~$8/mo) is marginally lower across the volumes we track, but the gap is small at low volume. The real decision is whether you want to run a server: happy to self-host → n8n (free software + your hosting); prefer a fully-managed cloud with a visual builder → Make. See the price table for figures; either way you won't overpay by much.
pairs.whyLoser: When you'd rather not run infrastructure. Make is fully managed, its free tier covers light use, and even at higher volume it stays modest — you trade a few dollars for zero ops burden and a polished visual builder.

pairs.verdict: Pipedream is the lower-cost option here, but the two lead with different defaults: Pipedream is code-first (every step can be Node/Python with full npm/PyPI access), while Zapier leads with a no-code point-and-click editor and 9,725 app connectors — it also has Code by Zapier (Python/JS) when you need a script. If your team writes code throughout, Pipedream offers more control for less; if you prefer building visually with code as the exception, Zapier's approach is what the price covers. See the price table for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When the people building automations don't code. Zapier's no-code editor, 9,725 app connectors and large template library let a marketer or ops person ship an automation alone — no engineering required.

pairs.verdict: Both are self-hostable, so philosophy doesn't separate them. Activepieces Cloud runs this at $0 (free up to 10 active flows, then $5 per flow, unlimited runs); n8n has the larger node ecosystem and more mature advanced logic, self-hosted from ~$8/mo. Start free on Activepieces if 10 flows is enough; move to n8n when you need its bigger toolkit. See the price table for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When automations get complex or numerous. n8n has no workflow cap (you pay only for the server), a larger node ecosystem, and more mature branching, error handling and code nodes — which start to matter once usage gets heavy.

pairs.verdict: Activepieces runs this at $0 (free up to 10 active flows, then $5 per flow, unlimited runs); Zapier's strength is its catalog — 9,725 app connectors vs Activepieces' 754 pieces. If your apps are covered by Activepieces' smaller, open-source catalog, it's the lower-cost option by a wide margin; if you need a niche integration only Zapier has, no discount replaces it. See the price table for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you need breadth or polish. Activepieces' 754 pieces cover the popular apps, but Zapier's 9,725-connector catalog is the deepest here — often the only one with a niche or regional tool — plus the largest template library and a no-code editor tuned for non-technical users.

pairs.seo_title: Make vs Pipedream — Pricing & Cost 2026 | WizardCost
pairs.verdict: Make is the lower-cost option across these volumes, and this time the no-code tool is the cheaper one. Pipedream is built for developers — workflows are Node/Python code steps with full npm/PyPI access — so it offers programmability Make's visual builder doesn't. Choose Pipedream if your team wants to write code; otherwise Make covers most needs for less. See the price table for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want real code. Pipedream runs Node/Python steps with npm and PyPI packages, an event-data inspector and an API-first design — capability that matters when logic gets genuinely complex.

pairs.verdict: Activepieces runs this at $0 (free up to 10 active flows with unlimited runs), while Make starts low and rises modestly with volume. The trade-off: Activepieces is open-source and self-hostable but free only up to 10 active flows; Make has the larger catalog (2,594 app connectors vs Activepieces' 754 pieces) and a more mature cloud. Pick by catalog coverage first — at these prices, cost is the tiebreaker, not the decider. See the price table for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want a bigger catalog and a polished, managed platform. Make has more integrations (2,594 app connectors vs 754 pieces), a more refined scenario builder, and a larger template and community pool, with modest, predictable costs.

pairs.seo_title: n8n vs Pipedream — Pricing & Cost 2026 | WizardCost
pairs.verdict: Both are developer-friendly, so this isn't no-code vs code — it's your own server vs managed cloud + code steps. n8n self-hosted is the lower-cost option if running a VPS is routine for your team (~$8–66/mo); Pipedream is fully managed with Node/Python code steps and event sources, so you never touch infrastructure. n8n Cloud is the managed comparison if you'd rather not self-host. See the price table for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you'd rather not run infrastructure. Pipedream is fully managed and scales without your attention, and its code-step model (Node/Python, npm/PyPI) is a powerful developer experience — teams that count engineering hours often prefer it to operating a server.

pairs.verdict: These two sit at opposite ends of the market. Automatisch is open-source and self-hosted, so across the volumes we track its cost is just the server it runs on, while Zapier is a fully managed cloud service priced per task with by far the larger catalog (9,725 app connectors vs Automatisch's 92). Automatisch trades breadth and convenience for data control and a flat running cost; Zapier trades higher pricing for reach and a no-code editor anyone can use. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When breadth and zero setup matter most. Zapier connects 9,725 apps — often the only tool that supports a niche or legacy system — and its point-and-click editor and template library let a non-technical person ship automations without running any infrastructure.

pairs.verdict: A managed SaaS service versus self-hosted software, for different audiences. Node-RED is open-source (Apache 2.0) and runs on your own hardware, so its cost is just that server; Zapier is hosted and priced per task, with a 9,725-app catalog and a no-code editor. Node-RED suits developers and IoT/hardware flows wired together in its visual editor; Zapier suits non-technical users connecting SaaS apps with nothing to host. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you're connecting SaaS apps without writing code or running servers. Zapier's 9,725 app connectors and point-and-click builder get non-technical users live fastest, with nothing to host or maintain.

pairs.verdict: Both lean visual, but the hosting model differs. Automatisch is open-source and self-hosted, so its cost is your server bill at any volume, while Make is a managed cloud builder priced per operation with a far larger app catalog (2,594 app connectors vs Automatisch's 92) and a polished drag-and-drop canvas. Automatisch trades integrations and convenience for data control and a flat cost; Make trades self-hosting for breadth and a richer editor. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want breadth and a polished builder without running servers. Make connects 2,594 apps with a visual, field-level editor and keeps a managed cloud running for you — a non-technical team can build complex scenarios without touching infrastructure.

pairs.verdict: Two visual tools with different roots. Node-RED is open-source (Apache 2.0), self-hosted and built for event-driven and IoT/hardware flows, so its cost is just your server; Make is a managed cloud platform priced per operation with 2,594 SaaS app connectors and a drag-and-drop canvas. Node-RED fits developers wiring devices and APIs; Make fits teams automating SaaS apps without hosting anything. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you're automating SaaS apps and would rather not host or code. Make's 2,594 app connectors, visual builder and managed infrastructure suit non-technical teams, where Node-RED's strengths are hardware, events and self-hosting.

pairs.verdict: Both are self-hosted, so on our figures they cost the same — the server they run on (see the table). The difference is scope: n8n carries a much larger node ecosystem (572 official nodes), native AI/LLM nodes and code steps, while Automatisch is deliberately minimal (92 connectors, no AI), AGPL-licensed and quick to stand up. Pick n8n for depth, Automatisch for simplicity and a lean footprint. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When your automations get complex or numerous. n8n has the larger node library, native AI/LLM steps, code nodes and more mature branching and error handling — depth that pays off once usage grows beyond simple flows.

pairs.verdict: Both are self-hosted and free to run, so our figures put them at the same cost — your server (see the table). They serve different builders: n8n is a general-purpose automation tool with 572 maintained official nodes, AI/LLM nodes and a visual editor aimed at business workflows, while Node-RED (Apache 2.0) is event-driven and excels at IoT/hardware, wired in a flow editor with Node.js function nodes and extended by 6,000+ community-published npm modules. The two count integrations on different bases — n8n's curated first-party nodes versus Node-RED's community modules — so the numbers aren't a like-for-like comparison. Pick n8n for SaaS automation, Node-RED for devices and events. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you're automating SaaS apps and APIs rather than hardware. n8n's 572 official nodes, native AI nodes and business-oriented editor cover that ground, where Node-RED leans toward IoT, events and low-level wiring.

pairs.verdict: Both are developer-friendly, but the cost and hosting models differ. Activepieces is MIT-licensed and runs free on its cloud free tier or self-hosted (cost is your server), while Pipedream is a managed cloud platform priced in credits once you pass its small free tier. Pipedream offers deeper code-first workflows (Node.js/Python with npm/PyPI); Activepieces offers a Zapier-like no-code UI plus self-hosting and an open license. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When your team writes code and wants a fully managed platform. Pipedream runs Node.js/Python steps with npm/PyPI packages, an event-data inspector and an API-first design — a powerful developer experience with no infrastructure to operate.

pairs.verdict: A code-first cloud platform versus a minimal self-hosted one. Automatisch is open-source and self-hosted, so its cost is your server bill, while Pipedream is managed and priced in credits, built for developers who write Node.js/Python in their workflows. Automatisch keeps things simple and EU-friendly with 92 connectors and no metering; Pipedream trades self-hosting for programmability and a larger catalog. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want managed, code-first automation. Pipedream lets developers run Node.js/Python with npm/PyPI, inspect event data and build API-first — without hosting or maintaining a server.

pairs.verdict: Both speak to developers, from different angles. Node-RED is open-source (Apache 2.0), self-hosted and event/IoT-oriented, so its cost is just your server; Pipedream is a managed cloud platform priced in credits, with Node.js/Python steps and a large SaaS catalog. Node-RED fits hardware and on-prem event flows; Pipedream fits cloud-hosted, code-first SaaS automation with nothing to operate. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want managed code-first workflows for SaaS. Pipedream runs Node.js/Python with npm/PyPI and connects a large app catalog without you hosting anything — where Node-RED's strengths are IoT, events and self-hosting.

pairs.verdict: Two open-source, self-hostable tools with different reach. Activepieces pairs an MIT license with a Zapier-like no-code UI and 754 pieces, and is free on its cloud free tier; Automatisch is AGPL-licensed, deliberately minimal (92 connectors, no AI) and simple to self-host. On our figures Activepieces runs at no cost on its free tier while Automatisch's cost is your server bill — see the table. Choose Activepieces for breadth and UI, Automatisch for a lean, EU-friendly footprint. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want the simplest possible self-hosted setup with full data control. Automatisch is quick to stand up, AGPL-licensed and unmetered — a lean fit when you only need a handful of integrations and want everything on your own server.

pairs.verdict: Both are open-source and self-hostable, aimed at different builders. Activepieces offers a Zapier-like no-code UI, 754 pieces and an MIT license, and is free on its cloud free tier; Node-RED (Apache 2.0) is a developer/IoT tool wired in a flow editor with Node.js function nodes. On our figures Activepieces runs at no cost on its free tier and Node-RED's cost is your server — see the table. Pick Activepieces for no-code SaaS automation, Node-RED for hardware and events. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you're working with IoT, hardware or event-driven flows. Node-RED's flow editor, Node.js function nodes and Apache 2.0 license make it the natural fit for device and on-prem automation, where Activepieces focuses on SaaS apps and a no-code UI.

pairs.verdict: Both are free, open-source and self-hosted, so our figures put them at the same cost — your server (see the table). They aim at different users: Automatisch is a simple, EU-friendly tool for basic SaaS automation (92 connectors, AGPL), while Node-RED (Apache 2.0) is a developer/IoT tool with a flow editor and Node.js function nodes. Pick Automatisch for simple flows you host yourself, Node-RED for hardware, events and code. See the price table below for figures.
pairs.whyLoser: When you want the simplest self-hosted setup for a few SaaS integrations. Automatisch is fast to stand up, EU-friendly and unmetered — a lean choice when you don't need code or hardware support and value data control.
